# Part A: Class codes

## 1. R as a calculator

```{r}
5 + 3; 10 / 4; 2^5; sqrt(81); log(100, base = 10)
```

## 2. Data structures

### Vectors

```{r}
age <- c(20, 35, 32, 29)
summary(age)
age <- c(35, 24, 18, 24)
mean(age)

x <- c(TRUE, FALSE)          # logical
class_g <- c("M", "F", "F", "M") # character
x <- 9:29                    # integer
x <- c(1 + 0i, 2 + 4i)       # complex
class(x)
```

### Matrix

```{r}
(x <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3))
(y <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2))
x %*% y
```

### List and factor

```{r}
(x <- list(1, "a", TRUE, 1 + 4i))
x <- factor(c("yes", "yes", "no", "yes", "no"))
table(x)
```

### Missing values

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 10, 3)
is.na(x)

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4, NA, 5)
y <- c("a", "b", NA, "d", NA, "f")
good <- complete.cases(x, y)
x[good]; y[good]
```

### Coercion

```{r}
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE))
class(c(1, "a", TRUE))
```

### Categorical vs continuous (iris)

```{r}
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
boxplot(Sepal.Length ~ Species, data = iris,
        main = "Comparison of categorical vs quantitative")
```

### Two categorical variables and Simpson's paradox

```{r}
ucba  <- data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
cross <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba)
prop.table(cross, 1)          # overall: men admitted more

cross2 <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba[ucba$Dept == "F", ])
prop.table(cross2, 1)         # in Dept F: women admitted more
```

### Bar charts

```{r}
dat <- read.table(text = "ProdA ProdB ProdC ProdD
1 110 50 60 70
2 120 50 80 65", header = TRUE)
barplot(as.matrix(dat), beside = TRUE, col = c("red", "green"))
```

### Scatter plot, correlation and linear model

```{r}
plot(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class)
abline(lm(WEIGHT ~ HEIGHT, data = data_class), col = "red")
lines(lowess(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT), col = "blue")
cor(data_class$HEIGHT, data_class$WEIGHT)

data_lm <- lm(HEIGHT ~ WEIGHT, data = data_class)
summary(data_lm)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(data_lm); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

hist(data_class$HEIGHT)
hist(data_class$WEIGHT, col = "blue")
```

```{r}
head(data_class, 5)
```

### Dates

```{r}
as.Date("2011-01-22") - as.Date("2004-02-13")
```

### Leadership data: missing values, categories, sorting, subsetting

```{r}
manager <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
country <- c("US", "US", "UK", "UK", "UK")
gender  <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "F")
age     <- c(32, 45, 25, 39, 99)
q1 <- c(5, 3, 3, 3, 2); q2 <- c(4, 5, 5, 3, 2); q3 <- c(5, 2, 5, 4, 1)
q4 <- c(5, 5, 5, NA, 2); q5 <- c(5, 5, 2, NA, 1)
leadership <- data.frame(manager, country, gender, age, q1, q2, q3, q4, q5)

leadership$age[leadership$age == 99] <- NA
leadership$agecat[leadership$age > 75] <- "Elder"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age >= 35 & leadership$age <= 75] <- "Middle Aged"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age < 35] <- "Young"
leadership

na.omit(leadership)                          # listwise deletion
leadership[order(leadership$age), ]          # sorting
leadership[c("q1", "q2", "q3", "q4", "q5")]  # select variables
subset(leadership, age >= 35 | age < 24, select = c(q1, q2, q3, q4, q5))
leadership[leadership$gender == "M" & leadership$age > 30 & !is.na(leadership$age), ]
```

### Merging

```{r}
extra <- data.frame(manager = 1:5, salary = c(5000, 6200, 4100, 5800, 7000))
merge(leadership, extra, by = "manager")      # horizontal
rbind(leadership[1:2, ], leadership[4, ])     # vertical
```

# Part B: ggplot2 geom functions

Data: `singer` from the **lattice** package, as used in class. It has the height (in inches) of 235 singers in a choir, and their `voice.part` (Bass, Tenor, Alto, Soprano).

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(lattice)
data(singer)
str(singer)
summary(singer$height)
```

### geom_bar()

**Aim:** count how many singers are in each voice part. `geom_bar()` counts the rows for us.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(voice.part)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Number of singers per voice part", x = "Voice part", y = "Count")
```

**What we see:** Bass 1 (39) and Soprano 1 (36) are the biggest groups. Tenor 1 and Tenor 2 are the smallest (21 each).

### geom_boxplot()

**Aim:** compare height between voice parts. A box plot shows the median, the middle 50% (the box) and outliers.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(voice.part, height)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(title = "Height by voice part", x = "Voice part", y = "Height (inches)")
```

**What we see:** height goes down from left to right. Bass 2 has the highest median (72 in), Soprano 2 the lowest (64 in). Lower voices belong to taller singers.

### geom_density()

**Aim:** show the shape of the height distribution as a smooth curve.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(height)) +
  geom_density(fill = "orange", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Density of singer height", x = "Height (inches)", y = "Density")
```

**What we see:** the curve has two bumps, near 65 and 70 inches. This suggests two groups mixed together (women in Alto/Soprano and men in Bass/Tenor).

### geom_histogram() with geom_vline() and geom_rug()

**Aim:** show how many singers fall in each height range. `geom_vline()` marks the mean, and `geom_rug()` puts a small tick for each singer under the x-axis.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(height)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(singer$height), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_rug() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of height (red line = mean)",
       x = "Height (inches)", y = "Number of singers")
```

**What we see:** heights go from 60 to 76 inches. The mean is 67.3 inches. Most singers are between 64 and 72 inches.

### geom_jitter() and geom_hline()

**Aim:** show every singer as a point. Many singers have the same height, so `geom_jitter()` moves points a little so they do not cover each other. `geom_hline()` draws the overall mean.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(voice.part, height)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(singer$height), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Jittered heights (dashed line = overall mean)",
       x = "Voice part", y = "Height (inches)")
```

**What we see:** Bass and Tenor points are mostly above the mean line. Alto and Soprano points are mostly below it.

### geom_violin()

**Aim:** compare the full shape of height in each voice part. A wide part of the violin means many singers have that height. A small box plot inside shows the median.

```{r}
ggplot(singer, aes(voice.part, height)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "plum") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Violin plot of height by voice part",
       x = "Voice part", y = "Height (inches)")
```

**What we see:** the same pattern as the box plot, but we also see where singers are most common. Tenor 1 and Alto 1 have the widest spread of heights (12 inches from shortest to tallest).

### geom_text()

**Aim:** put the exact value on top of each bar, so the reader does not need to guess.

```{r}
means <- aggregate(height ~ voice.part, data = singer, FUN = mean)
ggplot(means, aes(voice.part, height)) +
  geom_col(fill = "skyblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(height, 1)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(title = "Mean height per voice part", x = "Voice part", y = "Mean height (inches)")
```

**What we see:** mean height falls step by step from about 71 inches (Bass) to about 64 inches (Soprano).

### geom_line() and geom_point()

**Aim:** join the mean heights with a line to show the trend across voice parts. `geom_point()` marks each mean.

```{r}
ggplot(means, aes(voice.part, height, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(colour = "blue") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Mean height across voice parts", x = "Voice part", y = "Mean height (inches)")
```

**What we see:** a clear downward trend. The biggest drop is between Tenor 1 and Alto 2, which is where the choir moves from male to female voices.

### geom_point() and geom_smooth()

**Aim:** check the relationship between two numeric variables. Here we use the class height and weight data. `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` adds a straight regression line with its confidence band.

```{r}
ggplot(data_class, aes(HEIGHT, WEIGHT)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(title = "Weight vs height (class data)", x = "Height (cm)", y = "Weight (kg)")
```

**What we see:** the line goes up a little, so taller students tend to be a bit heavier. But points are very spread out (r = 0.27), so the relationship is weak.

## Conclusion

- Taller singers sing lower parts (Bass, Tenor). Shorter singers sing higher parts (Alto, Soprano).
- The height distribution has two peaks, because the choir has both men and women.
- In the class data, height and weight have a weak positive relationship (r = 0.27).
- Each `geom_*()` function shows the data in a different way. Choosing the right one depends on the question we want to answer.
